title: Trump: Saudi Crown Prince MBS brags that Jared Kushner is ‘in his pocket'
description_short: Trump: Saudi Crown Prince MBS brags that Jared Kushner is ‘in his pocket'
description_medium: In the last week of October 2017, Jared Kushner made an unexplained trip to Riyadh to meet Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. A source who spoke with confidants of Saudi and Emirati leaders later told The Intercept that MBS bragged to UAE Crown Prince Mohammed bin Zayed that Kushner was “in his pocket.” The source did not establish what the two discussed or whether the claim was true.
description_long:
Jared Kushner traveled to Riyadh during the last week of October 2017 for a meeting with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. The purpose and contents of the discussion were not publicly known. In the days afterward, a source who spoke frequently with confidants of Saudi and Emirati rulers told The Intercept that MBS had described Kushner as “in his pocket” to UAE Crown Prince Mohammed bin Zayed and others. The account is second-hand and does not independently confirm the alleged boast.

The linked timeline says MBS also claimed Kushner supplied names of Saudis disloyal to the regime. It notes that Saudi authorities soon arrested members of the royal family during an anti-corruption campaign, some of whom were reportedly named in a presidential intelligence briefing. The source raises the possibility that information was shared but does not establish that Kushner provided names or that the arrests resulted from the meeting.

The episode drew scrutiny because Kushner was a senior White House adviser meeting privately with a foreign leader who was consolidating power. The claim that he was “in his pocket” remains an attributed allegation, not proof of control, an exchange, or unauthorized disclosure.
organization_tags: Government of the United Arab Emirates

title: Trump Statement: This is a witch hunt, and I won the election
description_short: Trump Statement: This is a witch hunt, and I won the election
description_medium: After the Supreme Court allowed Manhattan prosecutors to obtain his accountants’ financial records, Donald Trump released a statement calling the investigation a “witch hunt.” He repeated claims that he had been cleared in the Russia investigation and said experts believed he had won the 2020 election. The statement attacked the Manhattan district attorney’s inquiry as politically motivated; it did not change the court’s order.
description_long:
The Office of Donald Trump issued a statement on February 22, 2021, after the Supreme Court declined to block the Manhattan district attorney from obtaining Trump’s financial records from his accounting firm. Trump called the investigation a “witch hunt” and described it as part of a broader effort by political opponents to target him. The statement referenced the Mueller investigation, his two impeachments, and the 2020 election.

Trump asserted that there had been “No Collusion” and claimed that many people and experts believed he had won the election. The latter repeated a false claim: Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election, and the result was certified. The statement framed the state investigation as a political attack and criticized the court for allowing prosecutors to seek records.

The event is a public response to a legal development, not a ruling on the merits of the Manhattan investigation. The Supreme Court order allowed prosecutors to pursue the records; Trump’s characterization did not reverse it. The record documents how he publicly challenged the investigation and repeated election claims after leaving office.

title: Trump: Roger Stone pulls Steve Bannon into his work with Julian Assange / WikiLeaks
description_short: Trump: Roger Stone pulls Steve Bannon into his work with Julian Assange / WikiLeaks
description_medium: On August 18, 2016, hours after Steve Bannon became Trump campaign manager, Roger Stone emailed him proposing a plan to help Trump win and said time was running short. Bannon replied that they should speak quickly. In later testimony, Bannon said he understood Stone’s reference to “new media” and “every tool” to include opposition research and possibly Stone’s reported WikiLeaks contacts; the email itself did not name WikiLeaks.
description_long:
Roger Stone emailed Steve Bannon on August 18, 2016, only hours after Bannon was named chair of Donald Trump’s campaign. Stone wrote that Trump could still win but time was short, and said he knew how to win although the approach “ain’t pretty.” Bannon replied that they should talk as soon as possible. The message referred to the campaign’s weakness in “new media” but did not explicitly mention WikiLeaks or Julian Assange.

In November 2019 testimony, Bannon was asked what he understood Stone to mean. He described Stone as an expert in opposition research and the tougher side of politics, and said a relationship with WikiLeaks or Assange was something he had been led to believe Stone possessed. His testimony documents Bannon’s understanding, not proof that the August email arranged a leak or that Bannon knew of any specific release plan at the time.

The exchange became relevant because Stone’s contacts and public statements about WikiLeaks were later examined in investigations of Russian interference. The email shows campaign officials discussing an urgent strategy and Bannon’s willingness to talk. It does not, on its own, establish coordination with WikiLeaks or the content of their subsequent conversation.

title: Trump: Denmark was poised to blow up airport runways if Trump attacked Greenland: REPORT
description_short: Trump: Denmark was poised to blow up airport runways if Trump attacked Greenland: REPORT
description_medium: In January 2026, Danish forces reportedly prepared to make Greenland’s airport runways unusable if the United States attacked the territory. Danish public broadcaster DR, citing officials, reported that troops brought explosives and blood supplies during Operation Arctic Endurance. BBC said the Danish defense ministry declined to comment, while the Financial Times reported that European officials confirmed the account. The report describes contingency planning, not an actual attack.
description_long:
Danish forces deployed to Greenland in January 2026 reportedly prepared for the possibility of a U.S. attack after President Donald Trump repeatedly discussed annexing the territory. Danish public broadcaster DR, citing government and military sources and European allies, reported that troops brought explosives to make key airport runways unusable and transported blood supplies to treat potential casualties. BBC coverage said the Danish defense ministry had no comment; the Financial Times reported that two European officials later confirmed the account.

The preparations were associated with Operation Arctic Endurance, a military exercise intended to protect Danish territory. The reporting describes a contingency measure in the event of fighting, not a plan to attack U.S. forces or evidence that an invasion was imminent. The supplied timeline links the episode to broader concern about Trump’s threats toward Greenland and Denmark’s status as a NATO ally.

The episode illustrates how public annexation rhetoric can affect allied security planning. The runway measure was reported rather than officially confirmed by Denmark, and the source does not establish that explosives were placed or that any attack order was issued. The distinction between reported contingency planning and actual military action is important.

title: Trump: Musk DOGE staffer with full access to Treasury payment system resigns over racist posts
description_short: Trump: Musk DOGE staffer with full access to Treasury payment system resigns over racist posts
description_medium: Marko Elez, a 25-year-old DOGE employee with access to the Treasury payment system, resigned on February 6, 2025, after the Wall Street Journal asked the White House about racist posts on accounts linked to him. The posts included calls for racial hatred and repeal of the Civil Rights Act. Elon Musk, Trump, and Vice President JD Vance later supported rehiring him. The episode raised concerns about staff vetting and access to federal payment infrastructure.
description_long:
Marko Elez, a 25-year-old staffer working with Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency, resigned on February 6, 2025, after the Wall Street Journal asked the White House about racist posts attributed to him. The posts included statements advocating hatred toward Indian people and repeal of the Civil Rights Act, as well as support for eugenic immigration policies. The linked account says Elez had access to the Treasury Department’s payment system, which processes large federal transactions.

The resignation was followed by a public discussion about whether he should return. Musk asked users on X whether DOGE should rehire Elez, and President Trump and Vice President JD Vance also supported reinstatement. The posts drew scrutiny because of both their content and Elez’s access to sensitive government payment operations.

The event raised questions about screening, accountability, and safeguards around systems that make federal payments. Access to a payment system does not establish that Elez changed or misdirected any payments; the supplied sources do not report such conduct. The record documents his resignation, the reported posts, and calls for rehiring, while keeping those issues separate from any claim of misuse of Treasury funds.

title: Travel Ban Expanded to 13 Countries Including Nigeria and Tanzania
description_short: Travel Ban Expanded to 13 Countries Including Nigeria and Tanzania
description_medium: In January 2020, the Trump administration expanded its travel restrictions to six more countries: Nigeria, Tanzania, Eritrea, Kyrgyzstan, Myanmar, and Sudan. The measure restricted immigrant visas for nationals of those countries, bringing the total number of countries affected to 13. Critics argued that the expansion disproportionately affected African and majority-Muslim populations and imposed costs on families seeking to reunite in the United States.
description_long:
The Trump administration announced an expansion of its travel restrictions in January 2020, adding Nigeria, Tanzania, Eritrea, Kyrgyzstan, Myanmar, and Sudan. The policy brought the number of countries affected to 13 and restricted immigrant visas for nationals of the newly listed countries. It did not impose an identical restriction on every type of travel, so the scope of the measure matters when describing its effects.

The expansion affected people seeking permanent immigration to the United States, including applicants with family ties in the country. Nigeria’s inclusion drew particular attention because it is Africa’s most populous country and largest economy. Critics argued that the policy extended restrictions to predominantly African and Muslim populations without a corresponding security justification. The Cato Institute concluded that earlier versions of the travel ban had produced little, if any, measurable security benefit while imposing humanitarian costs.

The change continued the administration’s use of nationality-based visa restrictions. Its practical impact depended on visa category, waiver availability, and individual circumstances. The supplied record describes the countries and policy scope, along with criticism of its rationale; it does not provide a full count of affected applicants or families.

title: Acting AG Rosen Pressured to Declare Election 'Corrupt' — Resists DOJ Coup Plot
description_short: Acting AG Rosen Pressured to Declare Election 'Corrupt' — Resists DOJ Coup Plot
description_medium: At a January 3, 2021, White House meeting, President Trump told Acting Attorney General Jeffrey Rosen and Deputy Attorney General Richard Donoghue to declare the election corrupt and leave the rest to him and Republican lawmakers. Rosen refused. Trump had also considered replacing Rosen with DOJ official Jeffrey Clark, who drafted a letter claiming election irregularities. Senior Justice Department leaders threatened to resign together, and Trump backed down.
description_long:
On January 3, 2021, President Donald Trump met with Acting Attorney General Jeffrey Rosen, Deputy Attorney General Richard Donoghue, and other officials at the White House. Contemporaneous Justice Department notes quoted in the January 6 committee report record Trump urging them to “just say the election was corrupt” and leave the rest to him and Republican lawmakers. Rosen and Donoghue refused to make that declaration.

Trump had separately been meeting with Justice Department official Jeffrey Clark, who drafted a letter asserting that DOJ had identified election irregularities in Georgia and urging the state legislature to appoint alternate electors. Trump considered replacing Rosen with Clark. Senior DOJ officials told the president they would resign en masse if he made the change, and Trump ultimately backed away.

The meeting was an attempt to use federal law enforcement authority to advance false claims about the 2020 election. The record is grounded in contemporaneous notes and congressional testimony. It documents pressure and a threatened leadership change, while showing that department officials resisted and that the contemplated replacement did not occur. It stands as a significant test of DOJ independence during the transfer of power.

title: Trump's Walter Reed COVID Treatment Used Experimental Drugs Unavailable to Public
description_short: Trump's Walter Reed COVID Treatment Used Experimental Drugs Unavailable to Public
description_medium: After testing positive for COVID-19, President Trump was hospitalized at Walter Reed on October 2, 2020, and received Regeneron’s experimental antibody treatment under compassionate use, along with remdesivir and dexamethasone. The antibody drug was still in clinical trials and not generally available. After leaving the hospital on October 5, Trump promoted the treatments without explaining that most patients could not access the same regimen.
description_long:
President Donald Trump was hospitalized at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center on October 2, 2020, after testing positive for COVID-19. His treatment included Regeneron’s monoclonal antibody cocktail, then known as REGN-COV2 and still in clinical trials, as well as remdesivir and dexamethasone. The antibody treatment was made available under a compassionate-use authorization. Trump left the hospital on October 5.

After his discharge, Trump publicly promoted the therapies and suggested that people could access them. The linked reporting emphasized that the experimental antibody treatment was not generally available and that compassionate use was an exceptional route. The record does not claim that every medication in Trump’s regimen was experimental or unavailable; the access disparity centered on the antibody cocktail and the level of care available to the president.

The episode highlighted differences between a president’s access to specialists and investigational treatments and the care available to ordinary patients during the pandemic. It also raised questions about how public officials communicate medical options during a public-health emergency. The supplied source documents Trump’s treatment and subsequent promotion, but does not assess the effectiveness of the full regimen for other patients.

title: Trump Invokes 1798 Alien Enemies Act for Mass Deportations
description_short: Trump Invokes 1798 Alien Enemies Act for Mass Deportations
description_medium: On March 14, 2025, President Trump invoked the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 to support deportations of Venezuelans the administration accused of belonging to Tren de Aragua. The move sought to use wartime authority outside ordinary immigration proceedings and was immediately challenged in court. The Act had been invoked during World War II, but its application to alleged gang activity and the administration’s claim of an invasion were disputed.
description_long:
President Donald Trump invoked the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 in March 2025 to authorize the removal of Venezuelan nationals whom his administration accused of belonging to the Tren de Aragua gang. The administration argued that the law’s wartime powers applied to the gang’s alleged activity. The measure sought to accelerate removals outside standard immigration-court procedures.

The law had previously been invoked during wartime, including against nationals of countries at war with the United States. Its use in this context was challenged because the United States had not declared war on Venezuela and legal experts questioned whether gang activity could satisfy the statute’s requirement of an invasion or predatory incursion. Courts immediately considered whether the president could make that determination unilaterally and what process affected individuals were owed.

The invocation raised questions about executive power and due process in immigration enforcement. The administration’s accusations against specific Venezuelans are not equivalent to individual findings of gang membership, and the supplied record does not resolve the litigation’s final outcome. The event is the invocation of an old statute for a new deportation policy, followed by immediate judicial scrutiny.

title: Steve Bannon Pleads Guilty in State Fraud Case, Avoids Jail
description_short: Steve Bannon Pleads Guilty in State Fraud Case, Avoids Jail
description_medium: On February 11, 2025, Steve Bannon pleaded guilty in Manhattan state court to a felony scheme-to-defraud count tied to the We Build the Wall fundraiser. He received a three-year conditional discharge and no jail time. The state case proceeded after Trump’s 2021 federal pardon, which did not cover state crimes. Manhattan prosecutors said donor money intended for the border-wall project had been diverted.
description_long:
Steve Bannon pleaded guilty on February 11, 2025, in New York state court to one felony count of scheme to defraud related to the “We Build the Wall” fundraising effort. The case concerned donations collected for a private border-wall project. Manhattan prosecutors said Bannon and others diverted more than $15 million intended for construction. Bannon received a three-year conditional discharge and no prison sentence.

The state prosecution followed a federal pardon Donald Trump granted Bannon in the final hours of his first term in January 2021. A presidential pardon covers federal offenses, not state charges, allowing Manhattan prosecutors to pursue a separate case. Two other defendants, Brian Kolfage and Andrew Badolato, had already been sentenced in related proceedings.

The plea established Bannon’s guilt on the state count and resolved the case without incarceration. The sentence differed from prison terms imposed on other participants, prompting attention to how the case treated each defendant. The record concerns donor funds and a guilty plea; it does not mean Bannon was convicted of every allegation made about the fundraising scheme or that Trump’s pardon erased the later state prosecution.
